legal.headline: CCCJFS at MNLU Nagpur organises National Conference on reimagining the organ transplantation regime in India
legal.hook: The conference brought together members of the judiciary and medical fraternity to deliberate on the legal, ethical and institutional challenges in India's organ transplantation framework
legal.summary: The conference brought together members of the judiciary and medical fraternity to deliberate on the legal, ethical and institutional challenges in India's organ transplantation framework CCCJFS at MNLU Nagpur organises a National Conference on reimagining India's organ transplantation regime and addressing key legal and policy issues. The Centre for Criminology, Criminal Justice and Forensic Science (CCCJFS), Maharashtra National Law University (MNLU), Nagpur, organised a National Conference on “Reimagining the Organ Transplantation Regime in India” on October 29-30, 2026. Kilor, Administrative Judge, Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, was the Distinguished Guest.
legal.contextNote: The article reports a conference organized by the Centre for Criminology, Criminal Justice and Forensic Science (CCCJFS) at Maharashtra National Law University, Nagpur, on 29‑30 Oct 2026, with Administrative Judge Kilor of the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, as Distinguished Guest. The piece frames the event as a high‑level dialogue between the judiciary and medical fraternity on legal, ethical and institutional challenges in India's organ transplantation framework. No specific statutory provision is cited, but the discussion is likely to touch on the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994 (as amended 2011) and the National Organ & Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO) guidelines. No precedent is directly referenced; the only court mention is the Bombay High Court bench hosting the judge.

legal.headline: NCDRC: Insurer’s internal coordination and administrative requirements no ground for condonation of delay; Explanation held to be an excuse
legal.hook: Neither of the documents indicate any change in the address of communication for summons and notices which remain intact under the policy schedule at the Prabhadevi Mumbai office
legal.summary: NCDRC holds that service at the address specified in the insurance policy was valid and rejects Bajaj Allianz's delayed written version beyond the 45-day statutory limit. National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: In an application filed by Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. (opposite party) seeking condonation of delay of 13 days in filing of the reply and praying to take it on record, A.P. Waaree Energies Ltd. instituted a consumer complaint against Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. The notice in the complaint was issued on 24 November 2025 and, according to the office report, was served on the insurer on 6 November 2025 at its Prabhadevi, Mumbai address.
legal.contextNote: The NCDRC rejected Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd.'s request to condone a 13‑day delay in filing its reply to a consumer complaint by A.P. Waaree Energies Ltd. The commission held that internal coordination and administrative lapses cannot justify missing the 45‑day statutory period for filing a reply under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The service of notice was deemed valid as it was sent to the insurer's registered address in Prabhadevi, Mumbai on 6 Nov 2025 and the complaint notice was issued on 24 Nov 2025. No precedent directly on point was cited; the decision rests on the statutory time‑limit provision of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

legal.headline: Dubai Arbitration Week 2026: Experts examine key reforms reshaping the DIFC arbitration and mediation framework
legal.hook: Experts examined changes concerning arbitral procedure, tribunal powers, emergency arbitration, enforcement of awards, and mediation settlements
legal.summary: Experts examined changes concerning arbitral procedure, tribunal powers, emergency arbitration, enforcement of awards, and mediation settlements Dubai Arbitration Week 2026: DIFC Courts' Chief Justice Wayne Martin and Justice Michael Black, DIAC's Robert Stephen, and Akin's Shane Jury and Michael Stewart examine proposed arbitration and mediation reforms. Dubai Arbitration Week 2026 , organised by the Dubai International Arbitration Centre (DIAC), is being held from 9 to 13 November 2026 . As part of Day 2 of the event, a session titled “Key Changes Under Proposed 2026 Reforms to the DIFC Arbitration Law and New DIFC Mediation Law” was held on 10 November 2026 .
legal.contextNote: An arbitration-law development. (1) Diarise the s.34 challenge window — three months from receipt of the award, extendable by 30 days — for any award a client holds or faces. (2) Where assets may be dissipated, s.9 interim relief is available before and during the proceedings. (3) Check the arbitration clause's seat and institutional rules, which decide the supervising court and the appointment route.

legal.headline: Claims prima facie factual: Delhi HC stays direction to remove “No Added Sugar”, “No Maida” and “No Palm Oil” claims from biscuit labels
legal.hook: The Court found no prima facie basis to say that such claims undermine other products or influence consumers
legal.summary: The Court found no prima facie basis to say that such claims undermine other products or influence consumers The Court allowed the petitioner to produce and market the product without the claim “100% Millets” as agreed by it. A show-cause notice was issued to the petitioner to provide reasons as to why the claim “100% Millets”, “No Added Sugar”, “No Maida” and “No Palm Oil” not be declared as misleading and not permissible under Regulation 6(1) of the 2018 Regulations . Aggrieved by the same, the petitioner filed the present writ petition.
legal.contextNote: The Delhi High Court dismissed the show‑cause notice that sought to bar the petitioner from using the claims “100% Millets”, “No Added Sugar”, “No Maida” and “No Palm Oil” on its biscuit packaging. The court held there was no prima facie basis to deem these statements misleading under Regulation 6(1) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2018. The petitioner may now market the product with the “100% Millets” claim as previously agreed. No prior precedent directly on these specific health‑claim labels was cited.

legal.headline: FSSAI milk logo: all milk and milk products to carry a prescribed logo from 1 July 2028
legal.hook: Composite milk products are covered, and minimum logo sizes are fixed for four display panel area bands
legal.summary: Composite milk products are covered, and minimum logo sizes are fixed for four display panel area bands FSSAI notifies Labelling and Display Second Amendment Regulations, 2026, requiring all milk and milk products to carry a prescribed logo from 1 July 2028. On 6 November 2026, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) notified the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2026 . The regulations will come into force on 1 July 2028, providing industry with a transition period before implementation. The Regulations are framed under Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 .

facts.label: Law
facts.value: s.92 Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

legal.contextNote: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) issued the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2026 under s.92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The amendment mandates that all milk and milk products, including composite milk products, display a prescribed logo. Minimum logo sizes are prescribed for four display‑panel area bands. The regulations become effective on 1 July 2028, giving the industry a transition window of 18 months from the notification date of 6 Nov 2026. No precedent directly on point; the nearest comparable requirement is the mandatory nutrition‑labelling order under the same Act.
